summary: Fire finder and training platform on a 1916 livery barn at the Darrington Ranger Station, used 1932 into the 1940s; the barn still stands, the platform's fate is disputed.

facts.design: Fire finder on a platform on the roof of the 1916 livery barn
facts.status_note: The barn still stands; sources disagree on whether the rooftop platform survives

access.note: The barn can be seen from Forest Lane and the Whitehorse Trail; SummitPost says going inside is generally not allowed

visit.trail_note: Drive along Forest Lane close to the barn, or park at the gravel lot for the Whitehorse Trail and walk a short distance

events.note: Livery barn constructed at the Darrington Ranger Station; the lookout platform came later
Lookout platform and fire finder on the barn roof; an August 1933 account describes a platform built on top of the barn
Used to train lookouts at the Forest Service's annual Fire School, paired with Whitechuck Bench Lookout; use ran through the 1940s
Platform abandoned or removed sometime in the 1940s (sources give no exact year; 1940 is the start of the decade)

corrections.why: The Washington list marks the site Abandoned, and the barn that carried the platform still stands.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: SummitPost and Discover Darrington place the rooftop platform in 1932; Firelookout.com dates use of the fire finder from 1932, not its installation; an August 1933 account describes a platform being built on the barn; TrailChick dates the training use from 1934. The story gives 1932 or 1933 for the platform and mentions the 1934 date.

SummitPost and Discover Darrington say the platform was abandoned or removed in the 1940s. TrailChick, which visited in 2018, describes an old fire platform on the barn, and Willhite says the barn once had one. The story says whether the platform survives is unclear.

notes_for_editor: The brief records the site as gone, but the barn still stands and the Washington list marks it Abandoned; the correction is proposed. Whether a platform survives is disputed: SummitPost and Discover Darrington say it was removed or covered in the 1940s, TrailChick (visited 2018) describes one. The public access level is inferred from directions and SummitPost's note on the interior. The 1916 barn date is the only firm construction date for the building.
